title: Maximum Distance in Arrays
description:
# Maximum Distance in Arrays

You are given `m` arrays. Each array is sorted in non-decreasing order.

Choose one integer from one array and one integer from a different array. The distance between two chosen integers `a` and `b` is `|a - b|`.

Return the maximum possible distance.

Because the two integers must come from different arrays, you may not use the first and last value of the same array as a pair, even if they are the global minimum and global maximum.

## Example 1:

**Input:** arrays = [[1,2,3],[4,5],[1,2,3]]
**Output:** 4
**Explanation:** Pick `1` from the first or third array and `5` from the second array.

## Example 2:

**Input:** arrays = [[1],[1]]
**Output:** 0
**Explanation:** The only possible pair has equal values from two different arrays.

## Example 3:

**Input:** arrays = [[1,100],[2],[3]]
**Output:** 98
**Explanation:** The values `1` and `100` are in the same array, so they cannot be paired. The best valid pair is `100` and `2`.

## Constraints:

* `m == arrays.length`
* `2 <= m <= 10^5`
* `1 <= arrays[i].length <= 500`
* `-10^4 <= arrays[i][j] <= 10^4`
* `arrays[i]` is sorted in non-decreasing order.
* There are at most `10^5` integers in all the arrays.

solutions.name: Track Global Min and Max
solutions.description:
## Approach

Scan arrays from left to right. Before updating the global minimum first value and global maximum last value, compare the current array's last value with the previous global minimum and compare the previous global maximum with the current array's first value.

## Key Insight

The order of operations enforces the different-array rule. At index `i`, the stored global endpoints come only from arrays `0..i-1`, so pairing them with the current array cannot accidentally choose two numbers from the same array.

## Complexity Analysis

Only the first and last value of each array are read. If `m` is the number of arrays, the time complexity is O(m), and the extra space complexity is O(1).

solutions.name: Sort Endpoint Candidates
solutions.description:
## Approach

For each array, record `(minimum value, array index)` and `(maximum value, array index)`. Sort minimum candidates ascending and maximum candidates descending. If the best minimum and best maximum come from different arrays, use them; otherwise try the two alternatives that replace exactly one endpoint with the next best candidate.

## Key Insight

A maximum distance always uses an endpoint: either a smallest first value or a largest last value. When the strongest endpoints come from the same array, only two second-best repairs can beat all other choices: keep the largest maximum with the second-smallest minimum, or keep the smallest minimum with the second-largest maximum.

## Complexity Analysis

Building candidate arrays takes O(m) time, sorting them takes O(m log m), and the final comparison is O(1). The candidate arrays use O(m) extra space.

solutions.name: Prefix and Suffix Extremes
solutions.description:
## Approach

Precompute the minimum first value and maximum last value available on each prefix and suffix of the array list. Then enumerate each array and combine its endpoints only with extremes from indices strictly before it or strictly after it.

## Key Insight

This route makes the different-array rule explicit. Instead of relying on update order, every candidate pair uses current index `i` on one side and prefix or suffix data that excludes `i` on the other side.

## Complexity Analysis

The algorithm scans the `m` arrays a constant number of times, so the time complexity is O(m). The four prefix/suffix arrays require O(m) extra space.
